terms.def: A programmable privacy network built on zero-knowledge proofs, designed for the next generation of compliant finance. Enables private transactions while maintaining regulatory compliance through selective disclosure.

The Miden Virtual Machine — a zero-knowledge virtual machine that enables private, verifiable computation. Built on STARK proofs, it allows users to execute programs locally and prove their execution without revealing inputs.

A blockchain architecture pioneered by Miden where computation and state changes happen on the client side (the 'edge'), rather than on a shared network. Transactions are executed locally and proven with ZK proofs.
An open-source STARK prover library created by Bobbin Threadbare, one of the fastest STARK implementations. The proving engine that powers Miden VM.
Miden's approach to managing user state. Accounts can hold complex state and execute arbitrary programs, enabling smart contract-like functionality with privacy.
Miden's transaction approach. Notes are private messages between accounts containing assets and execution scripts, enabling asynchronous private transactions.
Miden's approach where users execute transactions and generate proofs on their own devices rather than on a shared network, enabling privacy and scalability.
Merkelized Abstract Syntax Tree used in Miden for efficient code representation and verification.
The official name of the Miden protocol when it was part of the Polygon ecosystem, now independently developed.
The low-level programming language for the Miden VM, designed for writing efficient zero-knowledge programs.
A cryptographic method where one party can prove to another that a statement is true, without revealing any information beyond the validity of the statement itself.
Scalable Transparent ARgument of Knowledge. A type of zero-knowledge proof that is quantum-resistant, requires no trusted setup, and scales well for large computations.
Succinct Non-interactive ARgument of Knowledge. Produces very small proofs but most require a trusted setup and aren't quantum-resistant.
In zero-knowledge systems, the party that generates a proof to demonstrate knowledge or correctness of a computation without revealing underlying data.
In zero-knowledge systems, the party that checks a proof to determine if a statement is true. Verification is typically much faster than proof generation.
A zero-knowledge proof that verifies another zero-knowledge proof, allowing complex computations to be broken down into smaller combined proofs.
A mathematical representation of a computation that can be proven and verified. Programs are compiled into circuits that define computational constraints.
A one-time ceremony required by some ZK systems to generate initial parameters. If compromised, system security fails. STARKs don't require this.
The private input to a zero-knowledge proof that the prover knows but doesn't reveal to the verifier.
A cryptographic primitive allowing one to commit to a value while keeping it hidden, with the ability to reveal it later.
Fast Reed-Solomon Interactive Oracle Proof of Proximity, the core protocol underlying STARK proofs.
A popular SNARK proving system that allows for universal and updateable trusted setups.
A widely-used SNARK construction known for producing very small proofs and fast verification.
Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Argument of Knowledge, the full term for SNARK systems.
Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Argument of Knowledge, the full term for STARK systems.
Short non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs that don't require a trusted setup, used for range proofs.
A zero-knowledge proof that a value lies within a specific range without revealing the exact value.
The property that a proof system cannot convince a verifier of a false statement except with negligible probability.
The property that an honest prover can always convince a verifier of a true statement.
The property that a proof reveals nothing beyond the truth of the statement being proven.
A distributed ledger where transactions are recorded in cryptographically linked blocks. Each block contains a hash of the previous block, creating an immutable chain.
The mechanism by which nodes in a distributed network agree on the ledger state. Common mechanisms include PoW, PoS, and BFT.
Self-executing programs on a blockchain that automatically enforce agreements when predetermined conditions are met.
A measure of computational effort required to execute operations. Users pay gas fees to compensate network operators.
A layer-2 scaling solution that executes transactions off-chain and posts compressed data to the main chain.
The base layer of a blockchain network where primary consensus and validation occurs. Examples: Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana.
Scaling solutions built on top of L1 blockchains. Process transactions off-chain while inheriting L1 security.
Decentralized Application that runs on a blockchain or peer-to-peer network rather than centralized servers.
Ethereum Virtual Machine, the runtime environment for smart contracts on Ethereum and EVM-compatible chains.
Software or hardware storing private keys, enabling blockchain interaction, transaction signing, and account management.
A separate blockchain network for testing and development. Testnet tokens have no real value.
The live production blockchain where real transactions with actual value occur.
A service providing external data to smart contracts, bridging blockchains and the real world.
Automated Market Maker using liquidity pools and mathematical formulas to price assets instead of order books.
Funds locked in a smart contract enabling trading on decentralized exchanges. Providers earn fees from trades.
Multi-signature wallet requiring multiple private keys to authorize transactions, preventing single points of failure.
Protocol connecting different blockchains, enabling asset transfers and cross-chain communication.
A divergence in the blockchain where the protocol changes, creating two separate chains from a common history.
A protocol change incompatible with previous versions, requiring all nodes to upgrade.
A backward-compatible protocol change where old nodes can still validate new blocks.
The number of blocks in the chain between any given block and the genesis block.
The average time it takes to mine or produce a new block on the blockchain.
The point at which a transaction is considered irreversible and permanently recorded.
The pool of unconfirmed transactions waiting to be included in the next block.
A number used once in cryptographic communication, often to prevent replay attacks or as a counter.
The first block in a blockchain, hardcoded into the network software.
A web tool for searching and viewing blockchain data including transactions, blocks, and addresses.
A unique identifier (hash) for a blockchain transaction, used to track and verify it.
The current data set of all accounts, balances, and contract storage on a blockchain.
The process of moving from one blockchain state to another through transaction execution.
A separate blockchain connected to a main chain, allowing assets to move between them.
A framework for building scalable applications through child chains anchored to a main blockchain.
Off-chain communication between participants, only settling final state on-chain for scalability.
A rollup that assumes transactions are valid by default, using fraud proofs to challenge invalid ones.
A rollup using zero-knowledge proofs to verify transaction validity, offering stronger security guarantees.
A scaling solution using ZK proofs for computation validity while storing data off-chain.
A hybrid system allowing users to choose between on-chain and off-chain data availability.
The ability to transact or hold assets without revealing identifying information, amounts, or balances to unauthorized parties.
Revealing specific information to authorized parties while keeping other details private, critical for compliant privacy.
Miden's core feature allowing developers to define custom privacy rules for their applications.
Adherence to regulatory requirements, often involving KYC/AML and selective disclosure mechanisms.
A private exchange for trading large volumes without revealing orders to public markets.
A transaction where amounts are hidden using cryptographic techniques while still being verifiable.
A cryptographic signature scheme providing anonymity by hiding the actual signer among a group.
A one-time address generated for each transaction to prevent linking transactions to a recipient.
Combining multiple transactions to obscure the relationship between senders and recipients.
A service that mixes cryptocurrency from multiple sources to break transaction trails.
A privacy technique where multiple users combine their transactions into one to obscure ownership.
Using zero-knowledge SNARKs to enable private transactions with cryptographic proof of validity.
Encryption allowing computations on encrypted data without decrypting it first.
A privacy framework that adds noise to data to protect individual privacy while maintaining statistical accuracy.
Know Your Customer - identity verification processes required by regulations to prevent fraud and money laundering.
Anti-Money Laundering - regulations and procedures to detect and prevent money laundering activities.
Encoding information so only authorized parties can access it, protecting private keys and transaction data.
A mathematical function converting any input into a fixed-size output. Cryptographic hashes are one-way and collision-resistant.
The publicly shareable part of a key pair, used to verify signatures or encrypt data.
The secret part of a key pair used to sign transactions and prove ownership. Must be kept confidential.
A cryptographic mechanism proving a message was created by the holder of a specific private key.
A tree where each leaf is a data hash and each non-leaf is a hash of its children. Efficiently verifies data integrity.
Security against quantum computer attacks. Miden uses post-quantum cryptography (STARKs) for future-proofing.
Encryption using a public-private key pair, where one key encrypts and the other decrypts.
Encryption where the same key is used for both encryption and decryption.
Public key cryptography based on elliptic curves, offering strong security with smaller key sizes.
Secure Hash Algorithm producing 256-bit hashes, widely used in blockchain (Bitcoin, Ethereum).
The cryptographic hash function underlying SHA-3 and used in Ethereum.
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm used for signing transactions in many blockchains.
Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm, a modern signature scheme offering better performance.
A signature scheme enabling signature aggregation and multisignatures efficiently.
Boneh-Lynn-Shacham signature scheme allowing efficient signature aggregation.
Cryptographic operations requiring cooperation of multiple parties to prevent single points of failure.
Protocols allowing parties to jointly compute a function while keeping inputs private.
Dividing a secret into shares where a threshold number is needed to reconstruct it.
Random data added to inputs before hashing to prevent dictionary attacks.
Hash-based Message Authentication Code, combining a hash function with a secret key.
A function deriving one or more secret keys from a master secret.
A list of words encoding wallet private keys, allowing backup and recovery.
Hierarchical Deterministic wallet generating addresses from a single seed phrase.
Bitcoin Improvement Proposal defining the standard for mnemonic seed phrases.
Decentralized Finance - financial applications built on blockchain without traditional intermediaries.
Decentralized Exchange - a platform for trading cryptocurrencies without a central authority.
Providing liquidity to DeFi protocols to earn returns in the form of fees and tokens.
Locking tokens to support network operations (like validation) in exchange for rewards.
Penalty mechanism where staked tokens are destroyed for malicious or incorrect validator behavior.
A network participant who validates and adds new blocks to the blockchain in PoS systems.
A token holder who delegates their stake to a validator in PoS networks.
A consensus mechanism requiring computational work to validate transactions and create blocks.
A consensus mechanism where validators are chosen based on their stake in the network.
The process of validating transactions and creating new blocks in PoW blockchains.
A participant who performs mining in PoW networks, competing to solve cryptographic puzzles.
The computational power used for mining, measured in hashes per second.
A measure of how hard it is to mine a new block, adjusting to maintain consistent block times.
The cryptocurrency given to miners or validators for successfully creating a new block.
Periodic reduction in block rewards (Bitcoin), occurring approximately every 4 years.
A digital asset created on an existing blockchain, representing value or utility.
A cryptocurrency native to its own blockchain (Bitcoin, Ether, etc.).
Any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin.
A cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value, usually pegged to fiat currency.
A token granting holders voting rights on protocol decisions and upgrades.
A token providing access to a product or service within a blockchain ecosystem.
Non-Fungible Token - a unique digital asset representing ownership of specific items or content.
The Ethereum standard for fungible tokens, defining a common interface.
The Ethereum standard for non-fungible tokens (NFTs).
An Ethereum standard supporting both fungible and non-fungible tokens in one contract.
The maximum amount of gas a user is willing to spend on a transaction.
The amount a user pays per unit of gas, determining transaction priority.
A denomination of ETH equal to 0.000000001 ETH, commonly used for gas prices.
The smallest denomination of ETH, equal to 0.000000000000000001 ETH.
The smallest unit of Bitcoin, equal to 0.00000001 BTC.
Unspent Transaction Output - the accounting model used by Bitcoin and similar blockchains.
An accounting model tracking balances directly, used by Ethereum and Miden.
The cost paid to process a transaction on a blockchain, compensating validators.
Maximal Extractable Value - profit extracted by reordering, including, or censoring transactions.
Infrastructure to mitigate MEV negative effects and democratize extraction.
Placing a transaction ahead of another to profit from price movements it will cause.
An MEV attack placing transactions before and after a target transaction to extract value.
Decentralized Autonomous Organization - an organization governed by smart contracts and token holders.
The process by which protocol decisions and upgrades are made, often through token voting.
A suggested change to a protocol submitted for community voting in governance systems.
A tool for off-chain governance voting using token balances at a specific block.
A mechanism delaying execution of approved proposals to allow for community review.
A wallet requiring multiple signatures to execute transactions, enhancing security.
A cryptocurrency wallet not connected to the internet, offering maximum security.
A cryptocurrency wallet connected to the internet, offering convenience over security.
A physical device storing private keys offline, combining security with usability.
A physical document containing a public address and private key, completely offline.
A wallet where a third party (exchange, service) controls the private keys.
A wallet where the user maintains full control of their private keys.
The ability of different blockchain networks to communicate and share data.
Interactions or transactions occurring across different blockchain networks.
A peer-to-peer exchange of cryptocurrencies across different blockchains without intermediaries.
A token representing an asset from another blockchain (e.g., WBTC represents Bitcoin on Ethereum).
Maintaining a token's value relative to another asset, usually through collateralization.
The challenge of securely bringing external data onto a blockchain.
A decentralized oracle network providing external data to smart contracts.
An uncollateralized loan that must be borrowed and repaid within a single transaction.
Temporary loss experienced by liquidity providers when token price ratios change.
The total amount of assets deposited in a DeFi protocol, measuring its size.
The real rate of return earned on an investment, accounting for compound interest.
The difference between expected and actual transaction prices due to market movement.
How much a trade affects the market price, higher for larger trades in smaller pools.
A mathematical curve determining token price based on supply in automated market making.
Earning tokens by providing liquidity to a protocol, incentivizing participation.
Free distribution of tokens to wallet addresses, often for marketing or governance.
A list of approved addresses with special access or privileges in token sales or features.
A schedule controlling when tokens become available, preventing immediate selling.
A period during vesting where no tokens are released, followed by a partial or full unlock.
The design of a token's supply, distribution, and incentive mechanisms.
Permanently removing tokens from circulation to increase scarcity and value.
Creating new tokens, either as part of block rewards or token supply expansion.
The maximum number of tokens that will ever exist for a cryptocurrency.
The number of tokens currently available and trading in the market.
Total value of a cryptocurrency, calculated as price multiplied by circulating supply.
Market value if all tokens were in circulation, price times max supply.
How easily an asset can be bought or sold without significantly affecting its price.
A list of buy and sell orders for an asset, showing market depth.
An order to buy or sell at a specific price or better.
An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available current price.
An order that automatically sells when the price drops to a specified level.
Profiting from price differences of the same asset across different markets.
Two assets that can be traded against each other (e.g., ETH/USDC).
The asset being bought or sold in a trading pair.
The asset used to quote the price in a trading pair.
A price chart showing open, high, low, and close prices for specific time periods.
A market characterized by rising prices and investor optimism.
A market characterized by falling prices and investor pessimism.
Holding cryptocurrency long-term despite price volatility (originally a typo of 'hold').
Fear Of Missing Out - buying due to fear of missing potential gains.
Fear, Uncertainty, and Doubt - negative information spread to influence sentiment.
An individual or entity holding large amounts of cryptocurrency, able to influence prices.
Artificially inflating an asset's price to sell at profit, then causing a crash.
A scam where developers abandon a project and steal investors' funds.
Promoting a cryptocurrency or project for personal gain, often misleadingly.
Competition to get transactions processed by offering higher gas prices.
When an entity controls majority hash power and can manipulate the blockchain.
Using the same cryptocurrency units in multiple transactions, prevented by blockchain consensus.
Reorganization of blockchain history when a longer chain becomes the canonical one.
The specific method used to achieve agreement among distributed network participants.
A system's ability to reach consensus even when some nodes fail or act maliciously.
Creating multiple fake identities to gain disproportionate influence in a network.
Isolating a node by controlling all its network connections.
Sending tiny amounts of crypto to many addresses to de-anonymize users.
A record of when a block or transaction was created.
The process of spreading new blocks across the network.
In Ethereum, a valid block not included in the main chain but still rewarded.
A valid block not part of the longest chain, eventually discarded.
A point in blockchain history considered irreversible for security.
A node that doesn't store the full blockchain, verifying using block headers.
A node storing complete blockchain history and validating all transactions.
A full node also storing all historical states of the blockchain.
Removing old blockchain data to reduce storage requirements.
Splitting a blockchain into parallel chains to improve scalability.
The coordination layer in Ethereum 2.0 managing the proof-of-stake consensus.
The layer handling transaction execution and smart contract logic.
The layer managing block production and finality in blockchain systems.
Ensuring transaction data is accessible to verify blockchain state.
Data included with a transaction, often containing function calls and parameters.
Large data objects in EIP-4844 for cheaper rollup data storage.
An Ethereum upgrade introducing blob transactions for rollup scaling.
Full implementation of Ethereum sharding using data availability sampling.
Separating block proposal from block building to improve decentralization.
